paragraphs.text: Nos. 1–96 and 98–128 are from the writings of Eusebius.
No. 96 in part, and Nos. 97 and 129, are from Epiphanius, Panarion 72.

That no name among those ever named on earth has been greater than that of Jesus is attested by the Gospel, where "the angel" said to Mary: "Do not be afraid, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great, and will be called Son of the Most High." It is also clear from the prophecy of Zechariah, which long ago prophesied about this name. For he says: "The Lord showed me Jesus the high priest standing before the face of the angel of the Lord, and the devil was standing at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to the devil: The Lord who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you." When, then, did he rebuke him? When he joined to his own Word the man whom he loved. "He who has chosen Jerusalem," he says—clearly meaning our Jerusalem, of which the Apostle says: "But our Jerusalem is above; for she [?] is in slavery with her children." For it was then, when he had come into that great Jerusalem, that is, into our Church, that he rebuked the devil in accordance with the prophecy, saying: "Get behind me, Satan, for you are a stumbling block to me [?]." This, then, is the high priest, the great one, of whom the Jesus of that time preserved the type. For it was not possible for that man to be called great high priest, glorious as he had become in every respect, when Moses was not called great (and yet [?] Moses was great, for he was even called the servant of God, and was named god of [?] by God himself). But if anyone should think that Jesus was called great on the ground that he was counted worthy to lead the people into the holy land and performed many other wonders, let him recognize from this as well that the greatness ascribed to Jesus was distinguished not so much by the typical event itself as by its pointing to the one who, a little later, was to lead his own people into this great Jerusalem.

The apostle, then, says not only that he is the firstborn of the "new creation" but also the firstborn "from the dead." It seems to me that he does this for one reason only: so that through "firstborn of the dead" we may understand in what sense he is also called "firstborn of all creation." For our Lord Jesus Christ was not the first to rise from the dead. The man raised through the prophet Elisha rose before him, Lazarus rose before his resurrection, and at the time of the passion "many bodies of those who had fallen asleep" were raised.

Now let us examine a passage from what Asterius wrote. He said: "For the Father is indeed other, he who begot from himself the only-begotten Word and firstborn of all creation." He put both terms together and wrote "only-begotten" and "firstborn," although these names contradict each other sharply, as even very slow learners can easily see. Clearly the only-begotten, if he really is only-begotten, cannot also be firstborn, and the firstborn, insofar as he is firstborn, cannot be only-begotten.
So if he is "firstborn of all creation," and "in him all things were created," we should recognize that the apostle is speaking here of his dispensation according to the flesh.
He was therefore called "firstborn of all creation" because of his birth according to the flesh, not because of a first creation, as they suppose.

So this most holy Word was not called "firstborn of all creation" before the incarnation. How could one who always exists be the firstborn of anything? Rather, the divine scriptures give the name "firstborn of all creation" to the first "new man," the one in whom God willed "to sum up all things."
You hear how not only these things but also the things that already existed, "in the heavens and on the earth," turn out to have been "created in him" in the new creation.

And let Asterius not think it implausible that his body, though younger, could attain such antiquity. Let him rather consider this [?]: even if the human flesh is in fact younger, the Word who deigned to assume it through a pure virgin united it to himself. In doing so he not only made the man created in him "firstborn of all creation" but also wills him to be the beginning of all things, not only of those on earth but also of those in heaven.

So when this chapter of Proverbs said "The Lord created me," it did not mean to present the beginning of our Savior's divinity, as they think, but his second dispensation, the one according to the flesh. That is why it fittingly speaks of creation, the creation of human flesh.

So "creation" belongs to his activity as a man. That is why it says, "He created me as the beginning of his ways for his works." He created me, that is, through the virgin Mary, through whom God chose to unite human flesh to his own Word.

Since this is so, it follows that we should consider carefully this chapter spoken in proverbs: "He created me as the beginning of his ways for his works." The Lord God truly created, for he made what did not exist. The flesh that the Word assumed did not exist; when it did not yet exist, "he created it as the beginning of his ways."

Fittingly, then, when the old things had passed away and the new things, which were still to come, were not yet present [?] through the newness of our Savior, our Lord Christ cried out through the prophet, saying, "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways."
For he has become for us, who are to live righteously, the way of godliness, the beginning of all the ways that follow.

He fittingly called our Lord and Savior the "beginning of ways" because Christ also became the beginning of the other ways we have had after the first way. By these he means the traditions handed down through the holy apostles, who proclaimed this new mystery to us "with a lofty proclamation," as the prophecy says.

"He created me," then, it says, "as the beginning of his ways for his works." Which works does it mean? Those of which the Savior says, "My Father is working until now, and I am working," and again, "I have finished the work that you gave me."
For before the events proved it, who would have believed that the Word of God would be born through a virgin, assume our flesh, and display the whole Godhead bodily in it?

"Before the age he established me." Here he calls his dispensation according to the flesh, which had been foreordained, a foundation, as the apostle also says: "For no one can lay any other foundation than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ." Here it mentions a single age, from which it said the things concerning Christ had been founded, even though many ages had passed, as David said: "he who exists before the ages."

Asterius said that the Word was begotten before the ages, but the text itself convicts him of falsehood, so that he misses not only the substance but even the letter. For if Proverbs says, "Before the age he established me," how could he say that he was begotten before the ages? It is one thing for him to have been founded before the age and another for him to have been begotten before the ages.

Just as almighty God foreordained the church long ago, so he also first founded in his own mind the dispensation of Christ according to the flesh. Through Christ he foreordained that he would call the race of the godly "to adoption as sons." That is why the apostle, speaking by the Holy Spirit, clearly proclaims it in advance when he speaks "of the Son who was foreordained."

So even though this new mystery appeared at the end of the times, it had for that very reason been foreordained before this age. The prophet therefore fittingly said, "Before the age he established me." He means the flesh, because of its communion with God's true Son, the Word.

Then it says, "In the beginning, before he made the earth." What earth is this, if not our flesh, which became earth again after the disobedience? For "you are earth," it says, "and to earth you shall return." This earth had to be healed, having in some way shared in the holy [?]
Then it says, "before he made the depths." Here the prophet, speaking in proverbs, says that the depths are the hearts of the saints, which hold the gift of the Spirit in their depths.

What then does this chapter mean: "before the springs of waters came forth"? It says that these are the holy apostles. The scripture of Exodus presents this mystery to us, foretelling long ago the types of the apostles. Since the apostles are twelve in number, it mentions twelve springs.
Fittingly, then, the Lord spoke about his birth according to the flesh through the prophet Solomon, saying, "before the springs of waters came forth."
For this is how the Savior spoke to the holy springs: "Go and make disciples of all nations."
It is clear from every side that the prophet figuratively called the holy apostles springs.

Now that we have spoken about what comes first, it follows that we should complete what remains. What remains is the passage about the mountains and the hills. For it says, "Before the mountains were set in place, and before all the hills, he begets me." By mountains and hills he means the apostles and the successors of the apostles. In this way he signifies, in proverbs, their righteous way of life compared with that of other people.

For this reason it seems right to me now to go through matters I have not yet discussed, since most of what he wrote has become clear to us from what has already been said. "From the womb," it says, "before the morning star I begot you." He clearly thought that if he stole away the preposition "from," the text would agree with the opinion of the heresy. So by removing the most essential syllable he tried to make it signify his ancient regeneration [?].

How then can those who are "full of deceit and villainy," to use the apostle's words, transfer this text to what they suppose was his first creation, when David clearly said it about his birth according to the flesh?

Before this there was darkness, because people did not know how to worship God. But the day was about to appear ("For I am," he says, "the day"), and so he fittingly calls the star the "morning star."

The prophet David fittingly called the star that revealed the day the morning star. It is therefore no longer right to ask who this morning star might be, for it was the star that appeared at that time, bringing and revealing the day to the magi. It is quite clear, then, that the almighty Lord said "before the morning star I begot you" about the Word born through the virgin with human flesh. The Gospel clearly indicates this as well: first our Lord was born through the virgin, and afterward the star appeared that showed the day.

Otherwise, from which divine texts will they be able to show us that there is one unbegotten and one begotten, in the way they believe he was begotten, when neither prophets nor evangelists nor apostles have said this?

So the holy apostle and disciple of the [Lord], John, recalled his eternity and became a true witness to the Word, saying, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Here he makes no mention of a begetting of the Word, but by using three testimonies one after another he confirmed that the Word was in the beginning.

I will remind you of what he himself wrote in defense of what Eusebius had wrongly written, so that you may know that he clearly departs from his earlier profession. He wrote in these very words: "For the main point of the letter is to refer the Son's begetting to the will of the Father, and not to represent God's offspring as the product of passion [?]. The wisest of the fathers declared this in their own treatises, guarding against the impiety of the heretics, who falsely ascribed to God a bodily and passible begetting of children by teaching emanations."

So Asterius, wanting to defend Eusebius, who had written wrongly, mentioned the nature of a father and the nature of the unbegotten, and so became his own accuser. It would have been much better to leave the depth of Eusebius's thought unexamined, lying in its brevity, as he himself wrote, than to bring the craftiness of the writing to light by speculating in this way.

His statement that he was begotten before the ages seems consistent, for what has come forth from the Father who put it forth becomes his offspring. But he has not taken up the other point soundly or piously. To say that the one who came forth from him is not Word, and that this is not the true manner of the begetting, but that he is simply Son and nothing more, tends to give hearers the impression of something human.

Paulinus did not write these things by appealing to the teaching of the Gospel. Instead he admitted that some are moved this way of their own accord, while others have been led to this view by reading the men mentioned above. Then at the end, as if adding a crowning flourish to his demonstration, he appended passages from Origen to his letter, as though Origen could persuade better than the evangelists and the apostles. These are the passages: "It is time to take up again the subject of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and to go through a few of the things that were left out then. Concerning the Father: being indivisible and undivided, he becomes Father of the Son, not by putting him forth, as some think. For if the Son is something put forth by the Father and an offspring from him, like the offspring of animals, then both the one who put forth and the one put forth must be bodies."

Origen wrote these things because he did not wish to learn about the eternity of the Word from the holy prophets and apostles. Instead he gave himself too much freedom and vainly dared to describe a second hypostasis [?] of the Word.

In writing such things Origen was following his own opinions. This is clear from the fact that he often overturns his own views. It is fitting, at any rate, to recall what he says about God in another passage. He writes: "For God did not begin to be Father after being hindered, as men who become fathers are hindered by not yet being able to be fathers. For if God is always perfect, and the power to be Father belongs to him, and it is good for him to be Father of such a Son, why should he delay and deprive himself of the good, and, so to speak, from the time he is able to be Father, not [?]...? The same must also be said about the Holy Spirit." Origen wrote this too. How then did the man Asterius calls the blessed Paulinus think it safe to conceal this, while using contradictory statements to establish his own views? I would say that not even Origen himself could give an account of them.

Persuaded by these passages, Paulinus, Asterius's father, does not hesitate to say and write the same things. Sometimes he calls Christ a second God and says that he became God in a more human way; at other times he defines him as a creature. That this is so is shown by the fact that once, when he was passing through Ancyra, he told us too that Christ was a creature.

And that is why he does not call himself Son of God but everywhere calls himself Son of Man. Through such a confession he causes man to become Son of God by adoption, through communion with him. After the completion of his work, he will be united to God again as Word, fulfilling what the apostle said beforehand: "Then he himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all." For then he will be what he was before.

For the Word "was in the beginning," being nothing other than Word. But the man united to the Word did not exist before and came to be man, as John teaches us when he says, "And the Word became flesh." That is why John evidently mentions the Word alone. Whenever divine scripture mentions the name Jesus or Christ, it evidently names the Word of God as he exists with human flesh. And if anyone claims that he can show the name Christ or Jesus applied to the Word alone even before the new covenant, he will find that it was said prophetically, as this passage makes clear: "The kings of the earth stood up," it says, "and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ."

So it is clear from every side that no name suits the eternity of the Word except the one that John, God's most holy disciple and apostle, used at the beginning of the Gospel. After he assumed the flesh he is proclaimed Christ and Jesus, life, way, day, resurrection, door, bread, and whatever else the divine scriptures may call him. But that is no reason for us to be ignorant of his first name: he was Word. For this reason the most holy evangelist and disciple of the Lord, who was fully awake in the Spirit, recalled the beginning from above and nothing more recent. He said, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," to show that any new and more recent name came to him from the new and recent dispensation according to the flesh.

For Sabellius too slipped from the right faith and did not know precisely either God or his holy Word. Whoever did not know the Word was ignorant of the Father as well. For "no one knows the Father," it says, "except the Son," that is, the Word, since the Word by himself provides knowledge of the Father. In the same way he spoke to those Jews of that time who thought they knew God but rejected his Word, through whom alone God is known: "No one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son reveals him." Since it was impossible to know God in any other way, he teaches people to know him through his own Word. So Sabellius erred as well, because he did not know precisely the Father and his Word.
So let him learn that the Word of God has come. He is not a Word only by a loose use of the name, as they say, but is truly Word.
He is not called Word in a loose sense, even if those who teach otherwise burst with their lies. He is Word in the proper and true sense.

***** but those who teach them seem ashamed, as it were, to mention the Word, though all the divine scriptures proclaim him in this way. David says of him, "By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established," and again, "He sent his Word and healed them." Solomon says, "The wicked will seek me and will not find me, for they hated wisdom and did not choose the Word of the Lord." Isaiah said, "For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the Word of the Lord from Jerusalem." And again Jeremiah says, "The wise were put to shame, terrified and caught, because they rejected the Word of the Lord." And the prophet Hosea said, "They hated the one who reproves in the gates, and they abhorred the holy Word." Micah likewise mentions the Word and says, "Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the Word of the Lord from Jerusalem."

So before he came down and was born through the virgin, he was only Word. He himself has written that something came down "in the last days" and was born of the virgin. What else was it, before it assumed human flesh? It was nothing other than Word.
Fittingly, then, before his descent he was what we have often said: Word. After his descent and his assumption of the flesh he also received various titles, since "the Word became flesh."

For what other mystery was hidden, if not the mystery of the Word? This mystery was formerly so hidden "in God" that no one among the former people clearly knew the things concerning the Word. But now we enjoy the riches "of the glory" and of the hidden mystery.

But John, the holy apostle and disciple of the Lord, teaches clearly and expressly at the beginning of the Gospel. Speaking of one who was formerly unknown among people, he names him the Word of the Almighty and says: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." He indicates the eternity of the Word with more than one testimony.

By saying "In the beginning was the Word," he shows that the Word is in the Father in power, for God is the beginning of all things that have come into being, the one "from whom are all things." By saying "and the Word was with God," he shows that the Word is with God in activity, for "all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being." And by saying that the Word is God, he avoids dividing the Godhead, since the Word is in him and he is in the Word. For "the Father is in me," he says, "and I am in the Father."

What then [?] of the harmony of the Holy Spirit, which bears witness to the eternity of the Word through many different persons? That is why John begins from the eternity of the Word, saying, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." By using three testimonies one after another, he means to show the eternity of the Word.

What then was this that came down before he became man? He will surely say: spirit. If he wants to say it was anything else, the angel who said to the virgin, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you," will not allow him. And if he says it is spirit, let him hear the Savior saying, "God is spirit."

But it seems that the Father is in the Word, even if Asterius and those who think as he does disagree. This is the view of the inspired prophet Isaiah, who says through the Holy Spirit: "And they will worship you and pray to you, because God is in you, and there is no other besides you. For you are God." You see how he tears out by the roots the cunning villainy of those who teach otherwise.
Here too the prophet likewise speaks about the Word who assumed our flesh.
Spirit could never produce shadow. That God himself is spirit, the Savior said: "God is spirit." And that God is light, he himself teaches us, saying, "I am the light."

For which of the holy angels or of righteous men was trustworthy enough to undo the punishment that God had personally decreed for him? Only the Word himself could, who was present with God and shared in fashioning man. It was to him that the Father said, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness," for there was no other god able to share in the fashioning. "For I am," he says, "God first, and I hereafter, and besides me there is no other God." So there was no younger god, nor any other who was god "hereafter" and able to work together with God. But one might examine the divine action through a small human example from our own experience, as through an image. A skilled sculptor who wants to fashion a statue first considers its outlines and features within himself. Then he works out what breadth and height would be fitting and examines the proportion of the whole in each part. He prepares the suitable material, bronze, and forms the future statue in advance in his mind, so that he believes he sees it with his intellect. He is conscious that his own reason, his word, works with him; by it he reasons and by it he habitually does everything, for nothing comes to be without reason. Then, as he begins this work that can be seen and touched, he urges himself on as if speaking to another: "Come, let us make; come, let us fashion a statue." In the same way God, the Lord of all, when he made the living statue from earth, urged on no one else but his own Word, saying, "Let us make man." He did not do this in the same manner as with the other things, for the whole creation came to be by a word.

For God did not need, for his work of construction, some finished preparation such as material or any other human sort. He needed only this preparation in his own mind. Since it was impossible for God to think about the construction of heaven without the Word and the wisdom that belongs to the Word, it fittingly says, "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him."

For before the world existed, the Word was in the Father. But when Almighty God resolved to make all things in heaven and on earth, the coming-into-being of the world required an active energy. And for this reason, since there was nothing else besides God (for all things are acknowledged to have come into being through him), the Word then came forth and became the maker of the world, he who even before had been preparing it inwardly, in thought. So the prophet Solomon teaches us, saying, "When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him," and "when he made secure the springs of the earth beneath heaven, when he made strong the foundations of the earth, I was beside him, setting things in order; I was the one in whom he delighted." And the Father rightly delighted, since he was making all things with wisdom and power through the Word.

For just as everything that has come into being has come into being from the Father through the Word, so too the things spoken by the Father are made known through the Word. That is why the most holy Moses here calls the Word an angel: he appeared for no other purpose than to announce to Moses what he knew would benefit the children of Israel. And he knew that it would benefit them to believe that God is one. That is why he said to him, "I am He Who Is": to teach that there is no other god besides himself. This, I think, is easy for those of sound mind to grasp even from a small and humble example taken from our own life. For no one can separate a man's word from him in power and in hypostasis. A man's word is one and the same with the man, and is distinguished from him by nothing except the activity of the deed alone.

Here the Father says to Moses, "I am He Who Is," but plainly he says it through the Word. For whatever the Father says, he is everywhere seen to say it through the Word. This is clear from our own case too, so far as small things can be compared with great and divine ones. For we too do everything we wish to say and do, as far as we are able, by means of our own word.

Whom, then, does Asterius suppose to be the one who says "I am He Who Is": the Son or the Father? For he said that there are two hypostases, of Father and of Son. He looks to the human flesh which the Word of God assumed, forms this notion because of it, and so separates the Son of God from the Father as one might separate a son of man from his natural father.

If, then, he says that the Father spoke these words to Moses as one separating himself from the Son, he will be admitting that the Son is not God. For how can one who says "I am He Who Is" not also be granting that he calls himself "the one who is" in contrast to what is not? But if he claims that it is the Son, divided in hypostasis, who says "I am He Who Is," he will in turn be taken to say the same thing about the Father. And either of these is impious.

I begin, then, with the letter he wrote, in order to answer each of the things that were wrongly written. He has written that he believes in God the Father Almighty, and in his Son, the only-begotten God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit, and he says that he learned this pattern of piety from the divine Scriptures. When he says this, I wholeheartedly accept what he says, for this pattern of piety is common to all of us: to believe in Father and Son and Holy Spirit. But when, failing to aim at the divine power, he speaks to us in a more human fashion, by means of some artful theory, of the Father as Father and the Son as Son, it is no longer safe to praise such a theory. For it is through such a theory that the heresy they are now devising comes to grow, as I think is easy to show clearly from his own words. For he said that one must believe the Father to be truly Father, and the Son truly Son, and the Holy Spirit likewise.

For it is impossible for three hypostases, if they exist, to be united in a monad, unless the triad first had its origin from a monad. For the holy Paul said that those things which have no share in God's unity are summed up into a monad; for only the Word and the Spirit belong to God in unity.

If, then, the Word is seen to have gone forth from the Father himself and to have come to us, while the Holy Spirit, as even Asterius acknowledged, proceeds from the Father, and if again the Savior says of the Spirit, "He will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and declare it to you," is not the monad clearly and plainly seen here, by an ineffable principle, expanding into a triad and yet in no way admitting division? For if the Word proceeds from the Father, and the Spirit too is acknowledged to proceed from the Father, and again the Savior says of the Spirit, "He will take from what is mine and declare it to you," is it not obvious that some hidden mystery is being unveiled? For unless the monad, being indivisible, expanded into a triad, how could he say of the Spirit at one time that he proceeds from the Father, and at another, "He will take from what is mine and declare it to you," and again, after breathing on the disciples, say, "Receive the Holy Spirit"? For if the Spirit proceeds from the Father, how is it promised that he will receive this ministry from the Son? If they were two divided persons, as Asterius said, then necessarily either the Spirit, proceeding from the Father, would have no need of the Son's ministry (for whatever proceeds from the Father must be perfect, in no way needing help from another), or else, if he receives from the Son and ministers grace from the Son's power, he would no longer proceed from the Father.

But if the Gospel says that after breathing on the disciples he said, "Receive the Holy Spirit," it is clear that the Spirit went forth from the Word. How then, if the Spirit came forth from the Word, does the same Spirit in turn proceed from the Father?
So he has not spoken rightly or fittingly in saying that there are three hypostases, and he said it not once but a second time as well.
We know that the dispensation according to the flesh pertains to the man, but we believe that the eternity according to the Spirit is united to the Father.

For if the Spirit alone were being examined, the Word would rightly be seen to be one and the same with God; but if the addition of the flesh in the Savior is examined, the Godhead seems to expand in activity alone. So the monad is rightly and truly indivisible.

For Asterius declared the Father and the Son to be one and the same only in this respect, that they agree in all things. He spoke thus: "And because of the exact agreement in all words and deeds, 'I and the Father are one.'"

If, then, he himself says, "I came forth from the Father and have come," and again, "And the word which you hear is not mine, but the Father's who sent me," and "All that the Father has is mine," it is clear that he was right also to say, "The Father is in me and I in the Father," so that the Word who says this is in God, and the Father is in the Word, because the Word is the power of the Father. For a trustworthy witness has called him "the power of God and the wisdom of God." So it is not because of the exact agreement in all words and deeds, as Asterius said, that the Savior says, "I and the Father are one," but because it is impossible either for the Word to be divided from God or for God to be divided from his own Word. And if Asterius thinks the Savior said this because of their agreement in all things, and is unwilling to learn the truth by paying attention to the second dispensation, it is necessary to remind him how at times an apparent disagreement can be seen [?]. For that is what the texts teach us. What agreement was there at the time of the passion, when he says, "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass," and then adds, "Yet not as I will, but as you will"? To say first, "Let this cup pass," was not the speech of one in agreement; nor does what follows seem to have anything to do with agreement, for he says, "Not my will but yours be done, Father." You hear how the letter of the text shows an apparent disagreement, between one who wills and one who does not will. That the Father willed it is clear from the fact that what he willed came to pass; and that the Son did not will it is clear from his asking to be spared. And again he says, "I seek not my own will but the will of the Father who sent me." How then can he say that the Savior said "I and the Father are one" because of their agreement in all things?

How can the Son be in agreement with the Father, or the Father with the Son, when the Son says, "All that the Father has is mine"? To say "All that the Father has is mine" was plainly the speech of a Son taking more than his share from the Father. That is why, instead of saying "All that the Father has is shared," he said, "All that the Father has is mine." Yet it was not the mark of one in agreement to speak like this; he would have said, "All that the Father has is shared." For if the Acts of the Apostles, praising the agreement of those who were then coming to the faith, said, "They had all things in common," and if among human beings who are able to agree all things ought to be regarded as common, how much more ought the Father and the Son to share in fellowship, if they are divided into two hypostases? But as it is, in saying "All that the Father has is mine," the Son appears to be taking more than the Father; while in declaring that he is not master even of his own word, but that the Father is master of this too (for he says, "The word which you hear is not mine but the Father's who sent me"), he shows the Father taking away what belongs to the child. On Asterius's notion, both of these sayings appear inconsistent. For one who is in agreement ought not to snatch away what belongs to the other (for that, at least, [?]), but to regard what belongs to each as common. So whenever we look to the human flesh, we shall find that the Savior did not say "I and the Father are one" in the sense Asterius has written [?]. For it was not because of the exact agreement in all words and deeds, as he himself has written, that the Savior said, "I and the Father are one." If that were so, he would surely have said, "I and the Father agree with each other in all things." But as it is, he said, "I and the Father are one." So if there was some disagreement in those cases, and the Master must speak the truth, we ought to know precisely that whenever the Savior says "I and the Father are one," he says it not with regard to the man whom he assumed, but with regard to the Word who came forth from the Father. For if there seems to be any disagreement, it ought to be referred to the weakness of the flesh, which the Word assumed without having had it before. But if unity is spoken of, it is seen to belong to the Word. That is why he rightly said not only "I and the Father are one," but also, "Have I been with you so long, Philip, and you say, 'Show me the Father'?" Clearly he meant not with these eyes, but with the eyes of the mind, which are able to see intelligible things. For both the Father and his Word are invisible to the eyes of the flesh. So it was not because of their agreement in all things that he said this to Philip.

For he himself confesses it, saying, "The Father is in me and I in the Father." And that he did not say this casually or without purpose is clear also from another saying of the apostle. For the one who said, "One Lord, one faith, one baptism," also said, "one God and Father, who is over all and through all and in all." You see that even here he does not depart from harmony, but here too the same thing has happened: having said "one Lord," he then said "one God," so that when he mentions the one Lord he includes the Father as well, and when he speaks of the Father he bears witness that the Word of God is not outside him.

And if you also wish to hear another prophecy of the same prophet confirming to us that God is one: "I am God," he says, "the first, and for the things to come, I am." For "I" indicates a single person; the two expressions signify to us one person. Having said "I," he adds "am," so that through the two parts of speech, pronoun and verb, the monad of the Godhead is attested. And if he needs yet another testimony, I shall again cite for him the same prophet, who says, "I am first and I am after these things, and besides me there is no God." If Asterius, stumbling over the human flesh which the Word assumed for our sake, thinks that the Son is divided in hypostasis from the Father, as a son of man is, let him show us who it is that says these things; for here too the saying belongs to a single person. Who, then, is it who says, "There is no God besides me"? And let him hear another prophecy too, which says, "There is no one righteous and a savior besides me." If he thinks there are two gods, he must admit that the other is neither righteous nor a savior. And if he is neither righteous nor a savior, how can he still be God? For the prophecy declares one to be righteous and savior. And again he says, "Before me there was no other, and after me there will be none; I am God, and there will be none besides me who saves." And if he wishes to hear yet another prophetic text, spoken perhaps to him and to those who think as he does about the Godhead, let him hear Isaiah himself saying, "Repent, you who go astray; turn back in your heart, and remember the former things from of old, that I am God, and there is none besides me." He did not say "I am God" [?], so that also through the addition of the article he might clearly show that he is the one God. And what of the prophet Hosea? Does he not bear witness to the same things, saying, "I brought you up out of Egypt, and you shall know no god besides me, and there is no savior besides me"? And again Malachi says, "Did not one God create you? Is there not one Father of you all?" But perhaps Asterius will say that David said nothing about this, though he is the most ancient of the prophets after Moses, and that for this reason he is in doubt whether one ought to believe that there are two gods divided in hypostasis or not. So, to keep him from saying this, I think it fitting to show him David too, saying the same things as the holy men already mentioned: "Hear, my people, and I will speak to you; Israel, and I will testify to you. If you listen to me, there shall be no new god among you, nor shall you worship a foreign god. For I am the Lord your God." Is it not clear that he who points to himself and says "I am" is saying that there is only one God, that is, himself?

What then? If we did not attend to the Spirit and believe the monad to be indivisible in power, would we not be sinning, since the Word clearly teaches us, "You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone"? He proclaims the same thing through the Gospel according to Mark as well. When a certain scribe came to him and asked which was the first of the commandments, he answered him with these words: "First of all: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord, and you shall love the Lord your God with all your soul and with all your strength. This is the first; and the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. There is no other commandment greater than these. And the scribe said to him, 'Well said, Teacher; you have truly said that God is one and there is none besides him.'" Now the scribe, who was thought to have learned piety through the Law, is seen praising the Savior's saying, "Hear, O Israel," when he says "the Lord your God is one," and affirming with an oath that it was well said; for he says, "Truly you have said that God is one and there is no other besides him." But those who boast that they know the mysteries of the New Covenant—these men want to fashion a second God as well, separated from the Father in hypostasis and in power.

That the divine Scripture is accustomed to call the monad Lord and God has already become clear from what was said earlier, where God spoke to his servant Moses: "And God said again to Moses: Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you." You see how here, pointing out to us one person, he calls the same one Lord and God. And again Scripture likewise says, "And the Lord spoke all these words, saying: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods besides me." You hear how through the pronoun he declares that there is only one God. And again a little later he says, "I am the Lord your God," saying that he himself is Lord and God. And what do we learn through another scripture? "And you shall know today," it says, "and not be turned aside in your mind, that the Lord your God, he is God in heaven above and on the earth below, and there is none besides him." And again in the same book of Deuteronomy it says, "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind." And again in the same book: "See, see that I am, and there is no God besides me; I will kill and I will make alive; I will strike and I will heal." How then did Asterius, who professes to approach the holy Scriptures with simplicity and reverence, not know this passage, which says, "The Lord your God, he is God in heaven above and on the earth below, and there is no other besides him," and that "he is one" and "besides him there is no other"?

How then will the holy prophet Jeremiah not plainly refute him as a teacher of strange doctrine? For prophesying to us about the Savior, he spoke thus: "This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found out every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among men."

So even if someone says this, arguing that there is a first God and a second, as Narcissus has written in these very words: "For the one who says, 'Let us make man in our image and after our likeness,' does not allow it either [?]; that he and his Father are two we have heard in part, from the testimony of the Lord himself and of the holy Scriptures." If, then, Narcissus wishes on this account to divide the Word from the Father in power, let him know that the prophet who wrote that God had said, "Let us make man in our image and after our likeness," himself wrote, "And God made man."

For I came upon a letter of Narcissus, the head of the church of Neronias, which he wrote to a certain Chrestus, Euphronius and Eusebius. In it, when Bishop Hosius had asked him whether he too, like Eusebius of Palestine, says that there are two essences, I learned from what he wrote that he answered that he believes there are three essences.

For he dared to divide the Word of God and to call the Word another God, separate from the Father in essence and in power; and how great a blasphemy he has fallen into can be readily and clearly learned from the very words he wrote. He has written, in these very words: "Surely the image and that of which it is the image are not conceived as one and the same, but as two essences, two things and two powers, just as there are that many names."

But the apostle writes such things about the faith of the Galatians. Eusebius, however, twisting the apostle's meaning—the reason for which the apostle, on account of the cause stated above, said, "My children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you"—attacked the Galatians as not holding a right opinion about God. For the apostle was truly suffering sharp and bitter labor pains, he says, because he knew that the Galatians did not hold the same views about piety as he did, and did not speak of two essences, two things, two powers and two gods.

Eusebius of Caesarea has written in the same way, since he too holds the same opinion about gods as Paulinus and the outsiders. For he has written not as though God alone exists, but as though there is one who is the only true God. It was from this source, then, that Paulinus, the father of Asterius, learned to think that there are younger gods.

How, then, have these men not turned to the same most evil road as the outsiders and set out to teach and write the same things, with Eusebius speaking like Valentinus and Hermes, and Narcissus like Marcion and Plato?

But abandoning the true knowledge, he has now again displayed to us his artful theory. Unable to establish what he wants from the divine Scriptures, he runs back to the fathers he thinks most wise, saying, "what the wisest of the fathers declared in their own treatises." Asterius says that his own fathers made a declaration and wrote a dogma about God from their own choice. For the word "dogma" belongs to human will and opinion. That this is so is amply attested for us by the dogmatic art of the physicians, and attested too by the so-called <dogmas> of the philosophers; and that even now the decrees of the senate are called "dogmas of the senate," no one, I think, is unaware.

For, wishing to plead on behalf of Eusebius, who wrote the letter badly, he said first that Eusebius composed the letter without expounding the doctrine in the manner of a teacher, "for the letter was not written to the church or to the uninstructed, but to the blessed Paulinus"—and he called him blessed for this reason, that he held the same opinion as Asterius. Well then, since we have learned who Asterius's wisest fathers are, I think it fitting also to name the one who became the teacher of Paulinus and the others. For from Paulinus's letter the one who was his teacher too will become plain to us.

And yet, if one must tell the truth about Origen, this is what ought to be said. He had only just given up his philosophical studies when he chose to devote himself to the divine words, before he had an accurate grasp of the Scriptures. Because his secular education was so extensive and so ambitious, he began to write sooner than he should have, was led astray by the doctrines of philosophy, and on their account wrote some things that were not right. This is clear: still mindful of Plato's doctrines and of the distinction he draws between first principles, he wrote a book On First Principles and gave his treatise that title. The strongest proof of this is that he took the opening words and the title of the book from nowhere else than from words spoken by Plato. For he wrote at the beginning: "Those who have believed and been persuaded." You will find this phrase, worded in just this way, in Plato's Gorgias.

I ask those of the saints who read this to treat what I have said as the seeds and beginnings of an exposition, and to add further proofs to it, so that the intentions of those who pervert the faith may be exposed still more. For truly they "have forsaken" the God who begot them, "and have dug cisterns for themselves."

I think it fitting to say a few words about the image as well. For he has written: "But the one begotten from him is another, 'who is the image of the invisible God.'" Asterius mentions the image of the invisible God for this reason: to teach that God differs from the Word as much as a man is thought to differ from his own image.

That is why he fittingly adds, "who is the image of the invisible God." When did he become an image, if not when he took up the creature formed "after the image and after the likeness"? For before that, as I have often said, he was nothing other than Word.

So it is evident that before he took up our body the Word in himself was not the image of the invisible God. For an image must be seen, so that through the image what has so far not been seen can be seen.

How then could Asterius write that the Word of God is the image of the invisible God? Images show the things of which they are images even when those things are absent, so that through them the absent one seems to appear. But if God is invisible and the Word is invisible too, how can the Word in himself be the image of the invisible God when he himself is invisible? For what is not visible can never be made to appear through what is invisible.

(Re SiJ) Hence it is clear on every count that what the holy apostle called the image of the invisible God is the flesh that was added to the Word, so that through the visible the invisible might also appear. "He is the image," says the apostle, "of the invisible God." He is so now, that is, since he took up the flesh that was made after the image of God; then he became the true image of the invisible God. For if through this image we have been counted worthy to know the Word of God, we ought to believe the Word himself when he says through the image, "I and the Father are one." For no one can know either the Word or the Father of the Word apart from this image.

So too the apostle says, as we noted a little earlier, "he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." By the form of the servant he means for us the human flesh. When God our Master was forming it by his own wisdom, he said, "Let us make man after our image and likeness," rightly calling the human flesh an image. For he knew exactly that a little later it would be the image of his own Word.

What will he say to this, then? I do not think he has anything to say about it. Nor do I think he would openly and without disguise admit to others what he hides in his own mind, though it can clearly be learned from what he has written. For he says: "The Father who begot from himself the only-begotten Word, the firstborn of all creation, is another: alone begetting alone, perfect begetting perfect, king begetting king, lord begetting lord, God begetting God, the exact image of his essence and will and glory and power." These words plainly expose his corrupt opinion about the Godhead. For how can the one begotten as Lord and God, as he himself said just before, be the image of God? An image of God is one thing, and God is another. So if he is an image, he is not Lord or God but the image of the Lord and God; and if he is truly Lord and God, then the Lord and God can no longer be the image of the Lord and God.

So he would have him be none of the things he has just named, since he says he is the image of all of them. Then if he is the image of essence, he cannot be essence itself; if he is the image of will, he cannot be will itself; if the image of power, he is no longer power; and if the image of glory, he is no longer glory. For an image is not an image of itself but of something else.

What grieves us in the case of Asterius is not so much that he was led to write such things. It is that some of those reputed to preside over the church have also forgotten the apostolic tradition, preferred what is outside to what is divine, and dared to write and teach things of this kind, which cling no less to the error of the men already mentioned.

They ought instead to cry out to the Lord with tears and mourning: "We have sinned, we have acted impiously, we have broken the law," and we have done what is evil in your sight; and now we have repented and beg to receive your loving-kindness. That is what would have suited him; that is what it would have profited him to say, because of God's immeasurable goodness and love for mankind. And yet it would have been fitting for God, who cares for us with love and justice, to answer, saying: "If an enemy had reproached me, I would have borne it; and if one who hates me had boasted against me, I would have hidden from him. But you, a man of one soul with me, my guide and my close friend, who shared sweet food with me; in the house of God we walked in harmony." For we know that he is with us, his ministers, from his own words: "Behold," he said, "I will be with you all the days" of your life "until the end of the age." Then he would surely have gone on to add the words that follow those just quoted: "Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into Hades, for wickedness is in their hearts." For Scripture says that those who are dead in the ignorance of their impiety are swallowed up by Hades; they were in fact dead, even while they seemed to be alive.

For they want the Savior to be a man. This is clear from the way Eusebius craftily twisted the apostle's words to his own purpose. As if he wanted to give birth, after some long-standing labor, to a very great blasphemy, he "brought out of his own treasure," in the Savior's words, "what is evil." Wishing to show that the Savior is only a man, as if he were uncovering for us some great secret mystery of the apostle, he spoke as follows: "Therefore the divine apostle too, handing down to us most clearly the secret and mystical theology, cries out and proclaims, 'One God,' and then, after the one God, he says, 'one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.'" If, then, he says that he is a man, looking only at his economy in the flesh, he surely also concedes this: that one should have no hope in him. For "cursed," said the prophet Jeremiah, "is the man who puts his hope in man."

But the man just mentioned paid little attention to the holy prophets. As though he were expounding some secret and hidden theology of the apostle, he said, "One God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." And he who says these things, and boasts so loudly of his memory of the Scriptures, failed to notice that the most holy apostle who wrote this also wrote: "who, being in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, coming to be in the likeness of man, and being found in appearance as a man." Do you see how the holy apostle, as if he foresaw their villainy in the Spirit, wrote in another passage "as a man" and "coming to be in the likeness of man," so as to strike down this enormous blasphemy of theirs?
How then can Eusebius ignore these words and want the Savior to be only a man? He does not dare to say so openly, but because this is what he wants, he is refuted by his own words.

Before all creation there was, as is reasonable, a kind of stillness, since the Word was in God. For if Asterius believes that God is the maker of all things, he will clearly agree with us that God always exists and never received a beginning of being, while all other things were made by him and made from nothing. I do not think he believes the one who says that some things are also unbegotten; rather, I think he is firmly convinced that heaven and earth and everything in the heavens and on earth were made by God. If, then, he believes this, he must also admit that apart from God there was nothing else. The Word, therefore, had his own glory, being in the Father.
Asterius calls the authority given to him glory, and not just glory but glory before the world, not realizing that before the world came into being there was nothing else but God alone.

For the man received authority not only over affairs on earth but also over those in the heavens, and reasonably so. For if, when he became both "man" and "mediator between God and men," "all things were created" for him, as the apostle said, "things in the heavens and things on earth," then it follows that we should know clearly that authority has been given to him not only over what is on earth but also over what is in the heavens.

For if the holy Gospel speaks of some glory given to him by the Father, it is evident that the man received it through the Word. Having become, as the holy apostle says, "mediator between God and men," he glorified God-fearing people with the glory given him by the Father.

And he counted the man who had fallen through disobedience worthy to be joined to his own Word through the virgin. What greater glory could there be among human beings than this glory? Having said, "I have glorified you," he adds, "and I will glorify you again." In his surpassing love for mankind, he meant that in the second glory, after the resurrection of the flesh, the man who was formerly mortal would be set free as immortal, and that he would glorify him with such glory that he would not only be freed from his former slavery but also be counted worthy of a glory beyond what is human.

so that, as I said, he might enable the man who had formerly been deceived by the devil to conquer the devil himself in turn. This is why he took up the man: so that he might then enable him to receive the firstfruits of authority.
(Re 35 = 97) For this is the beloved, the man united to the Word, of whom the evangelist said, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

that the Word of the invisible God was to be born through a virgin and to take up human flesh, so that, having overcome through it the devil who had formerly prevailed over man, he might make man not only incorruptible and immortal but also enthroned with God in the heavens.

So he who came down and took on flesh through the virgin was appointed king over the church, clearly so that the man who had formerly fallen from the kingdom of heaven might be able to obtain a kingdom through the Word. God wished that this man, who had formerly fallen from the kingdom through disobedience, should become Lord and God, and so he brought about this economy. Accordingly the most holy prophet David says prophetically, "The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice."
(Re lOU) For this reason the prophecy says, as though Christ our Master received the beginning of his kingship at a particular time, "But I have been appointed king by him."

This is why he will reign, having come in human flesh. And the man who was formerly deceived, having been appointed king through the Word, "will abolish every rule" of the devil, "and every power and authority." "For he must reign," he says, "until he has put his enemies under his feet." The holy apostle therefore says that the end of the kingship of Christ our Master is this: that all things should be subjected under his feet.
Here the apostle uncovers for us a very great mystery when he says that there will be an end to Christ's kingship, and that the end will come when all things have been subjected under his feet.

In our earlier passages we said, using proofs from the divine Scriptures, that Christ our Master had a beginning of his kingship. One text says, "But I have been appointed king by him on Zion, his holy mountain"; another says, "The Lord has become king; let the peoples rage"; and again, "The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice." In short, one could easily supply countless texts as testimony to show that the man received a beginning of kingship through the Word. If, then, he received the beginning of his kingship not more than four hundred full years ago, it is not surprising that the apostle says that the one who obtained this kingship so short a time ago will hand over the kingdom, clearly to the God who, as Scripture says, appointed him king.

So it appears that he has been separated from the Father in activity alone, on account of the flesh, until the coming time of judgment appears. Then those who pierced him will, as the prophecy says, see the one they pierced, and what remains will follow in due order. For when all things are to be subjected to Christ at the time of the end, as the apostle said, then "he himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him." What, then, do we learn about the human flesh which the Word took up for our sake not quite four hundred years ago? Will the Word keep it in the ages to come as well, or only until the time of judgment? For what the prophet said must be confirmed in fact: "They will look," he says, "on him whom they pierced"; and what they pierced was clearly flesh.

That the Word took up our flesh not to benefit himself, but so that the flesh might obtain immortality through its communion with the Word, is clear from the Savior's own statement. Speaking of the flesh he had while he lived among his disciples, he says: "Does this offend you? What then if you see the Son of Man going away to where he was before? The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing." If, then, he admits that the flesh profits him nothing, how is it possible that what comes from the earth and profits nothing should remain with the Word in the ages to come, as if it were of use to him? This is why, it seems to me, God Almighty, the Master, says to him, "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." Seeming to separate him in activity alone on account of the human flesh, and as though fixing for him a set time for sitting at his right hand, he says to him: "until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." And the holy apostle, interpreting this prophetic saying of David more clearly for us, put it something like this: "For he must reign until he puts his enemies as a footstool for his feet." So his economy and kingship as man appear to have a limit. For this saying of the apostle, "until he puts his enemies as a footstool for his feet," means nothing else. So when he has his enemies as a footstool for his feet, he no longer needs this partial kingship, since he is king of all things without exception; for he reigns together with "God the Father," whose Word he was and is. For it was not the Word in himself who received a beginning of kingship. Rather, the man who was deceived by the devil became king through the power of the Word, so that, having become king, he might conquer the devil who had formerly deceived him. This is why the Acts of the Apostles teaches as follows about this man, whom the Word of God took up and with whom he now sits at the right hand of the Father: "whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration." The Acts speaks in this way as if setting a limit and appointed term within which the economy as man must remain united to the Word. For what else does "until the times of restoration" mean, if not to point us to a coming age in which all things must attain complete restoration? Paul said that at the time of the restoration of all things the creation itself will also be changed from slavery to freedom, for he says "that the creation itself will be set free from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God." If so, how could the form of the servant which the Word took up, since it is the form of a servant, still remain with the Word? The inspired Paul has therefore said clearly and expressly that the economy of the Word in the flesh took place for our sake in a brief span of time between the past and future ages, and that, just as it had a beginning, so it will also have an end. He put it something like this: "Then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father."

Touching his human body and showing it to those who were looking on, he said: "Does this offend you? What then if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing."

Therefore he took up human flesh not for his own sake but for ours. And if he clearly took it up for our sake, and everything that concerns us will reach its end through his providence and activity at the time of judgment, then there will no longer be any need even for this partial kingship.

But if someone should say that the human flesh is worthy of the Word because he made it immortal through the resurrection, let him know that not everything immortal is worthy of God. For God is greater even than immortality itself, since by his own will he can make immortal even things that do not exist. That not everything immortal is worthy to be united with God is also clear from the fact that principalities, powers and angels, though they are immortal, have no part in [?] the unity of God.

But if someone should ask about this flesh which became immortal in the Word, what do we say to him? We say that we do not think it safe to lay down doctrine about things we have not learned precisely from the divine Scriptures. How could people who are overturning the doctrines of others do such a thing? But to those who want to learn from us the exact account of this matter, we will say that, in obedience to the holy apostle, we know that we are to see the hidden mysteries in the way he described: "For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face; now we know in part, but then we shall know fully, even as we have been fully known." So do not ask me about things I have not clearly learned from divine Scripture. For this reason I will not be able to speak clearly about that divine flesh which shared in the divine Word either. For now, I believe the divine Scriptures: that God is one, and that his Word came forth from the Father so that "all things" might come into being "through him." And after the time of judgment, the setting right of all things, and the destruction of every opposing power, "then he himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him," "to God the Father," so that the Word may be in God just as he was before the world existed. For when nothing existed except God alone, and all things were to come into being through the Word, the Word came forth with active power, this Word being the Father's own.
(above 109) This is the one of whom Paul said, "concerning the Son of God who was foreordained."
(above 110) For this reason the most holy prophet Solomon said, "to understand the twists of words," and again, "the sayings of the wise and their riddles,"
(above 111) That is why, it seems to me, this most wise prophet spoke even the first words of his prophecy in proverbs.
(above 112) For I think there is nothing out of place in reminding you here of a few proverbs from outside the Scriptures.

"EITHER HE IS DEAD OR HE IS TEACHING LETTERS." Going by the surface meaning of the words, one might suppose that this proverb was aimed at people who teach letters, since another of their writers also said, "You taught letters, and I went to school." But those who wrote the commentaries said that this is not the case. According to them, the Sicilians, after defeating the Athenians in war, spared only those who claimed to be educated, and took them away to be teachers for their children; all the rest they killed. When some of these men escaped and came home, and the Athenians asked them about certain people who mattered to them, they are said to have answered, "EITHER HE IS DEAD OR HE IS TEACHING LETTERS."

And what about "THE GOAT [FOUND] THE KNIFE"? One might think, to give first what is said about it, that the proverb was surely coined because the goat being sacrificed looks at the knife. But the ancients said nothing of the kind. If that were its meaning, which is what one would naturally gather from the surface of the words, it would not have been a proverb at all. Rather, they say it is used of those who bring harm on themselves. For they say that Medea, after killing her children in Corinth, hid the knife there. Later the Corinthians, following an oracle given to them, were offering a black goat to the dead but had no knife; and the goat, scratching with its hoof, dug up Medea's knife and was sacrificed with it.

And what does "ENOUGH OF THE OAK" mean? someone asks, for the proverb cannot be understood at first glance. The ancients, as they tell it, lived on acorns before grain was farmed. Since, as they believed, this crop was discovered later, they turned their attention to it and, glad of the change, said "ENOUGH OF THE OAK!" And this, they said, is the proverb.

Again, there is another proverb, mentioned by a great many of their wise men in many different books, and it is necessary at this point to recall what those who undertook to interpret proverbs have written about it, [?] but so that we may refute Asterius, who from his secular learning knows perfectly well what is peculiar to the proverb, but has at present pretended ignorance, so that he may appear to build up his own case plausibly by using the proverbial expression. The proverb is "THE ART OF GLAUCUS." The secular wise men who mention this proverb have explained it in different ways. One of them said that a certain Glaucus was skilled in some art [?] most marvelous, and that it perished with him at sea, since no one had yet learned it from him. Another, testifying to Glaucus's consummate skill in music, says that he made four bronze discs that, when struck, produced a harmonious concord of tones, and that the proverb arose from this. Someone else says that among the offerings of Alyattes there was dedicated a marvelous mixing bowl with its stand, the work of Glaucus of Chios. Another says that Glaucus himself dedicated at Delphi a bronze tripod, so crafted that, [?] when it was struck heavily, the feet on which it stands, the part lying above, the rim around the cauldron, and the rods set between them all sounded with the voice of a lyre. And yet another says that the proverb was coined from a certain Glaucus who was thought to have achieved something beyond the ordinary.

You see how the difficulty of the proverb is shown by this too: those who wanted to explain it could not even settle on the same interpretation. So hard to discover does the sense of a proverb seem to be, even among the outsiders. That is why one of their wise men collected the proverbs spoken by many people in various forms and wrote six books on them, two on those in verse and four on those in prose. And in my opinion the outsiders called these sayings "proverbs" for no other reason than this: they came upon the Proverbs of the most wise Solomon and learned from them that nothing said in them can be clearly understood at first glance; wishing to emulate the prophetic writing, they wrote in the same manner as he did; and then, unable to think of a more fitting name than his, they called these proverbs too.
(See above, 113.) So this is the meaning of "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works."
(See above, 114.) (He said) that the Word of God made human flesh immortal through the resurrection, and that, having put it on like a crown of victory, he sits at the right hand of the Father.
(See above, 115.) (Having composed a single . . . treatise, this [?] for the purpose of making God known.
Marcellus to the most blessed fellow minister Julius, greetings in Christ.

Certain men who were previously condemned for not believing rightly, and whom I refuted at the Council of Nicaea, have dared to write to Your Godliness against me, claiming that I do not think rightly or in accordance with the Church, in their eagerness to shift their own guilt onto me. For this reason I thought it necessary to come to Rome and to ask you to summon those who wrote against me, so that when they came I might convict them on both counts: that what they have written against me is false, and that even now they persist in their former error and have dared to commit terrible acts against the churches of God and against us who preside over them.

Since, then, they refused to come when you sent presbyters to them, and this although I have spent a whole year and three months in Rome, I thought it necessary, now that I am about to leave, to hand you a written statement of my own faith, set down with all truthfulness in my own hand, the faith I learned and was taught from the divine Scriptures. I also thought it necessary to remind you of the wicked things they say, so that you may know by what words they seek to conceal the truth and deceive their hearers. For they say that the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, is not the proper and true Word of the almighty God, but that God has another Word and another Wisdom and Power, and that this one, having been made by him, was named Word and Wisdom and Power. And because they think this way, they say that he is another hypostasis, separate from the Father. Moreover, they declare in their writings that the Father exists before the Son, and that the Son is not truly Son from [?], and even if they say "from God," they say it in the sense in which all things are from God. Further still, they dare to say that there was a time when he was not, and that he is a creature and a thing made, thus dividing him from the Father. I am therefore convinced that those who say these things are strangers to the Catholic Church.

But I believe, following the divine Scriptures, that there is one God, and his only-begotten Son, the Word, who always coexists with the Father and has never had a beginning of existence, who is truly from God, not created, not made, but always existing, always reigning together with God the Father, "of whose kingdom," according to the testimony of the apostle, "there will be no end." He is Son, he is Power, he is Wisdom. He is the proper and true Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, the indivisible Power of God, through whom all things that have come into being were made, as the Gospel testifies when it says: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being." This is the Word of whom Luke the evangelist also testifies, saying: "just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the Word handed them down to us." Of him David too said: "My heart has poured forth a good word." So also our Lord Jesus Christ teaches us through the Gospel, saying: "I came forth from the Father and have come." He it is who "in the last days" came down for our salvation, was born of the Virgin Mary, and took on humanity.

I believe, then, in God almighty; and in Christ Jesus, his only-begotten Son, our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried, and on the third day rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of the Father, from where he is coming to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit, the holy Church, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life. We have learned from the divine Scriptures that the Godhead of the Father and of the Son is indivisible. For if anyone separates the Son, that is, the Word, from the almighty God, he must either think that there are two gods, which is held to be foreign to divine teaching, or confess that the Word is not God, which is also plainly foreign to the right faith, since the evangelist says, "and the Word was God." But I have learned precisely that the Son, as Power, is indivisible from and inseparable from the Father. For the Savior himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, says: "The Father is in me, and I am in the Father," and "I and the Father are one," and "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." This faith, which I have received from the divine Scriptures and been taught by our godly forebears, I preach in the Church of God, and I have now written it to you, keeping a copy of it myself. And I ask you to include a copy of it in your letter to the bishops, so that none of those who do not know us well may pay attention to what those men have written and be deceived.
Farewell.
